tip: Dovunque (wherever) takes the subjunctive, not the indicative: 'dovunque tu sia', not 'sei'.
The future can express a guess about the present: 'avrà quarant'anni' means he's probably about forty.
tenere has an irregular future: the stem contracts to terr-, giving 'terrò', not 'tenerò'.
'Venire a trovare' is the idiom for visiting someone: 'verrò a trovarti' = I'll come see you, not find you.
'essere in vacanza' takes no article: 'sarò in vacanza' = I'll be on vacation, literally 'in vacation'.
'Entro' (by a deadline) pairs with the future perfect: 'saremo tornati' = we'll have returned by then.
dovere builds its future by dropping the stem vowel: 'dovrò', not 'doverò'.
'il che' refers back to a whole statement, meaning 'which': 'non ha chiamato, il che è strano'.
'farcela' means to manage or pull it off; the 'ce la' is fixed: 'ce la farò' = I'll make it.
Real condition: use the present after 'se' (dormi) and the future in the result (sarai stanco).
Unreal present: 'se' plus the imperfect subjunctive (avessi) with the conditional (comprerei) for a hypothetical.
With time words, 'in cui' means 'when/on which': 'la sera in cui', not 'la sera che'.
'che' serves as both subject and object relative and never changes: 'la storia che mi ha raccontato'.
After 'quando' about the future, Italian uses the future perfect: 'quando avrò finito' = when I've finished.
'quello che' (or 'ciò che') means 'what/that which': 'tutto quello che vuole' = all that he wants.
After a preceding object pronoun the participle agrees: 'l'' stands for la lettera, so 'spedita', feminine.
Past unreal: 'se' plus the pluperfect subjunctive (avessi saputo) with the past conditional (sarei venuto).
The future perfect can express a guess about the past: 'avranno già cenato' = they must have already eaten.
In questions the future signals wondering: 'dove saranno finiti?' = where could they have ended up?
'a casa' means 'at home' with no article: 'rimarrò a casa' = I'll stay home.
Use 'in' with countries and regions: 'in Grecia', 'in Italia'. Cities instead take 'a'.
Reciprocal reflexive: 'ci' means 'each other', so 'ci rivedremo' = we'll see each other again.
'sposarsi' (reflexive) = to get married; 'sposare' plus an object = to marry someone. Here 'ti sposerai'.
Graduating is reflexive in Italian: 'laurearsi', so 'mi laureerò' = I'll graduate.
'Chi' here means 'whoever/anyone who' and always takes a singular verb: 'chi studia... ottiene'.
For places, 'dove' can act as the relative 'where/in which': 'l'ufficio dove lavoro'.
Unlike English, Italian may use the future after 'se' for a real future case: 'se continuerà a piovere'.
Trapassato prossimo with avere: 'avevo letto' = I had read, an action finished before another past point.
'in punto' after a time means 'sharp/on the dot': 'alle dieci in punto' = at ten sharp.
